claims.text: The Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti baseline has a nearly BCC matrix.
The baseline lacks controlled nanoscale precipitate formation.
Warm forging at approximately 1000–1100 °C will refine the alloy microstructure.
Brief aging at approximately 700–800 °C after forging will precipitate nanoscale B2 or L12 particles.
The treatment will produce a uniform dispersion of coherent B2 or L12 precipitates within the nearly BCC matrix.
The nanoscale precipitates will impede dislocation motion.
The nanoscale precipitates will stabilize grain boundaries at high temperature.
Impeded dislocation motion and grain-boundary stabilization will elevate high-temperature yield strength.
Impeded dislocation motion and grain-boundary stabilization will reduce high-temperature creep rates.
A low precipitate volume fraction and coherent precipitate character will preserve at least 90% of the baseline room-temperature ductility.
A low precipitate volume fraction and coherent precipitate character will prevent a significant increase in alloy density.
Relative to an as-cast or single-step heat-treated baseline, the processed alloy will have approximately 10–20% higher yield strength at around 1100 °C.
The processed alloy will maintain at least 90% of the baseline room-temperature ductility.
The processed alloy will have no more than a 5% density increase relative to the baseline.
The proposed improvement should hold at temperatures of at least 900 °C, particularly near 1100 °C under tensile and creep loading.
Processing time, temperature, and cooling rate may require adjustment to obtain uniform precipitates without unwanted phase transformations.
The long-term stability of the precipitates under cyclic turbine loading is not established.
